chunks: "Swiss cheesing is when you put so many vias through a plane that the clearance holes around them, the antipads, cover so much of it that it looks like Swiss cheese.
It typically happens under a BGA or a dense connector, especially when the vias are in straight rows so the holes line up and the gaps between them merge into a slot.
The harm is that a plane stops behaving like a solid sheet.
The copper between holes becomes narrow necks, so resistance goes up and current crowds, which causes IR drop and hot spots on a power plane. The plane inductance goes up.
And a ground plane with slots forces return currents to detour around them, so the loop areas grow, and crosstalk and radiation get worse, especially if a fast trace crosses the slot.

To avoid it I stagger the via rows, use smaller pads and antipads, leave copper bridges, share ground vias, move vias out of the critical current area, or use blind and microvias that don't cut every layer."
